notes.meaning: David states a simple rule: God deals with people the way they deal with him. To people who keep their hearts clean, God shows his own pure goodness. To twisted people, God is 'shrewd.' He meets their twisting by letting them follow their own crooked ways until those ways bring them down. This is not God lying or tricking anyone. It shows his justice, and no one can fool him.

Here the rule is applied to God's people. The 'afflicted' are the humble, godly people who are pushed down. The 'haughty' are the proud and powerful who ignore God. God rescues the first and keeps his eye on the second to humble them. Elsewhere the Bible puts it this way: God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

David calls the LORD his lamp. When David was lost or low, God showed him the way and lifted him up into honour. God also promised to keep shining his saving light into David's dark times. Light comes first, because strength is little use if you can't see where you are going.

With God's help, David could rush against a troop of soldiers and climb over a city wall. In plain words, God's strength let him overcome every enemy in his way. One man alone should not be able to do this. The strength came from the Lord.

God's way of helping his people never fails. His word has been tested like pure, refined silver, and not one promise has burned away. People often promise and don't follow through, but God finishes what he starts. He is a shield for everyone who runs to him and trusts him.

There is no other true God who can help besides the LORD. The gods other people worship are fakes. A 'rock' is a picture of a high cliff where you are safe. Only God is a rock like that, strong and lasting.

God is David's strong fortress, a safe place no enemy can break into. He also leads David along his road and clears it of things that would trip him up. God gave David success in what he set out to do.

A deer runs fast and leaps over rocks without slipping. God gave David that kind of speed and sure footing when he faced his enemies. The 'heights' stand for both safety and honour. God set David firmly over his own land.

David was raised as a shepherd, yet God trained him for war. A bow made strong with bronze was very hard to bend, so bending one showed great strength. David gives God the credit for his skill and his strength.

God's 'shield of salvation' is his helping grace, which guarded David. David also says God's gentleness made him great. God's tender mercy, not David's own power, raised him to honour. God is so great he could crush us, but instead he bends down to lift up the lowly.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew here is slightly different from Psalm 18. Some read it as 'your answering' instead of 'your gentleness.' On that reading, God made David great by answering his cries for help.

notes.meaning: God gave David room to move, like widening a narrow trail. He cleared away the things that could make him stumble. So David's ankles held firm and he did not slip.

David remembers his victories over enemies like the Philistines, Moabites and others. The wins were quick and complete, and his foes could not get up again. Some teachers also see David looking ahead here. They hear in these lines the final defeat of all the enemies of God's kingdom.

'Armed me with strength' pictures a soldier tying up his clothes to get ready for hard work. David says it was God who did this. God made his enemies bow down and turn and run. David knows God was the true source of every victory.

David's enemies looked everywhere for help, even to the LORD, but no help came. They were not on God's side. They only cried to him when they were at the very end, and by then it was too late. They were crushed as small as dust. In this way God set up the rule of David's throne.

David's troubles did not come only from foreign nations. His own people fought him too: Saul's son Ishbosheth, his own son Absalom, and Sheba. God brought him through those fights and kept him to rule over other nations. Even far-off peoples David had never known came to serve him.

Just hearing reports of David's victories made foreign peoples give in, often without a fight. Some of them obeyed only on the outside, not from the heart. They lost hope of standing against him and came out of their hiding places shaking. Matthew Henry sees a picture here of Jesus, the Son of David, whose good news keeps winning more and more people.

'The LORD lives!' is a cry of praise. David's God is alive and at work, unlike the dead idols of the nations. David blesses God as the rock who saves him. God took up David's cause, put down nations under him, lifted him above his enemies, and saved him from violent men. All the glory for the victory belongs to God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters hear 'The LORD lives' as a cheer like 'Long live the king!' Older commentators reply that such a cheer only fits a human king, not the living God.

notes.meaning: God's kindness to David was too big to keep inside Israel. So David promises to praise God among the nations. As David's rule spread, so did the knowledge of his God. Paul later quoted this verse in Romans to show that God's salvation was meant for non-Jewish people too.

The song ends with God's faithful love for his 'anointed,' the king God chose and set apart. The word is 'messiah' in Hebrew. The last line echoes God's promise in 2 Samuel 7 that David's family would rule forever. That promise finds its goal in Jesus Christ, the Son of David, whose kingdom never ends. David closes not by leaning on his own goodness but by resting on God's mercy.
